source.title: A New Paradigm for Scattering Theory of Linear and Nonlinear Waves: Review and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Can stable self-similar weakly localized solutions for dispersive or hyperbolic wave equations be constructed in dimensions below five, and can one prove in such dimensions that relevant solutions decompose into a free wave plus a weakly localized part rather than collapsing to a purely localized state? The setting includes mass-critical behavior, possible saturation of nonlinearities, and the need to determine whether such solutions have physical significance and whether they undermine the inverse-scattering principle that asymptotic data determine the system.

evidence.quote: While the current method of construction applies only in five or more dimensions, it is anticipated that similar results hold in any dimension. In any dimension, the mass-critical equation possesses a self-similar solution. One must properly saturate the nonlinearity to obtain a stable solution. The decomposition into a free wave and a weakly localized part remains valid, at least in three dimensions and higher (in the spherically symmetric case). However, one must demonstrate that certain solutions do not collapse to a purely localized form. It may be simpler to generate more examples by considering systems of equations. The physical significance of such solutions hinges on the type of models exhibiting such behavior. This also raises questions about the validity of the Inverse Scattering Meta-Theorem.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a localized time-dependent breather solution in higher spatial dimensions for a dispersive or hyperbolic wave equation? More concretely, can one construct such a higher-dimensional breather either through a nonlinear equation, a system of coupled equations, a suitable dispersion relation with spectral gaps, or even a linear problem with a time-dependent potential and a localized time-dependent spatial solution?

evidence.quote: Simply stated: Does there exist a breather solution in higher dimensions? The standard ”soliton resolution conjecture” says no. But of course, this can only be generically true.

The problem can be further simplified by asking for a linear problem with a time-dependent potential and a localized time-dependent spatial solution, in higher dimensions, see also Plum and Reichel (2022).

accepted.question_text: For a regular bounded potential V(x,t) that is localized in space and positive but may depend on time, can the time-dependent Schrödinger equation i∂tψ = -∆ψ + V(x,t)ψ have localized solutions? In the broader formulation, if the frozen operator -∆ + V(x,t) has no bound states for every fixed time t, must the full time-dependent equation have no localized solutions in any spatial dimension?

evidence.quote: 14.2. Quantum Ping-Pong. This is another fundamental question with a straightforward formulation: Can a positive potential, which is localized in space, bounded, and a regular function, have bound states? Such a potential must be time-dependent.

The broader question is: assuming the operator − ∆ + V (x,t ) has no bound states for each fixed t, does it follow that the equation i∂ψ ∂t = − ∆ψ +V (x,t )ψ has NO localized solutions? This remains an open problem in any dimension.

accepted.question_text: For a time-independent positive localized potential V(x), can one prove for large data that the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation i∂tψ = -∆ψ + V(x)ψ + |ψ(x,t)|²ψ has no localized solutions? Small-data cases are known from Lp estimates for the linear part, but the open case concerns large bounded solutions that are known only to converge to a free wave plus a weakly localized component in dimensions three and higher.
accepted.context_brief: Large-data defocusing NLS without localized states

evidence.quote: A simplified version of this problem is as follows: prove that the equation below has no localized solutions for a time-independent V that is positive as described. For small data, this is known, utilizing the Lp estimates for the linear part. Our analysis demonstrates that for large data, all bounded solutions of this equation converge to a free wave plus a weakly localized solution in three or more dimensions. It’s noteworthy that the nonlinear term is defocusing. i∂ψ ∂t = − ∆ψ +V (x)ψ + |ψ (x,t )|2ψ.

accepted.question_text: For coupled systems in which one unknown ψ satisfies i∂tψ = -∆ψ + V(x)ψ + F(x,t,u)ψ and u is governed by another equation, how can one identify mathematically interesting coupled models, prove a priori estimates tailored to those models, and define channel wave operators for each unknown such as ψ and u so that the large-time decomposition into a free wave plus a weakly localized part can be established?

evidence.quote: This raises the question of how to identify interesting models of systems of equations and establish a priory estimates tailored to the system. In particular, it may be necessary to devise a suitable definition of channel wave operators for each of the unknown functions ψ,u .

accepted.question_text: For a dispersive equation with a mass-critical nonlinear term that is saturated by an additional term, or with an energy-critical term with saturation, can there exist global self-similar solutions? The issue is whether saturation can prevent blow-up while preserving asymptotic mass-critical or energy-critical scaling strongly enough to support self-similar dynamics.

evidence.quote: 14.4. Self-Similar Solutions. The fundamental question to address is whether self-similar solutions exist for a given dispersive equation with a mass-critical term that is also saturated with an extra term. The same question can be posed about energy-critical terms with saturation
Since one can choose the nonlinear term to be asymptotic to a mass-critical equation after scaling, the question arises: can there be a self-similar solution in this scenario?

accepted.question_text: In very long-range N-body scattering, when two-body interaction terms decay like |x|^-µ with µ ≤ √3 - 1 and standard proofs of asymptotic completeness break down, can one prove asymptotic completeness and determine whether new scattering channels with self-similar weakly localized solutions are required?

evidence.quote: In the study of N-body scattering, it is observed that if the two-body interaction terms vanish as |x|− µ , where µ ≤ √ 3 − 1, the proofs of Asymptotic Completeness (AC) break down. This occurs because the asymptotic dynamics of some channels are governed by time-dependent potentials, resulting in a self-similar spreading part due to the concentration of the solution at zero frequency over time. The community generally believes that AC holds in these cases but lacks a formal proof. Based on the analysis outlined here, it is conceivable that in the very long-range case, new scattering channels may emerge, featuring self-similar weakly localized solutions.

accepted.question_text: Can the three-quasi-particle scattering approach be extended to the N-body quasi-particle case by proving existence of the free channel wave operator and proving absence of weakly localized solutions for initial data in the continuous spectral subspace of the Hamiltonian? The expected difficulty is the need for many new propagation estimates.

evidence.quote: 14.5. N-Quasi-Particles. We have demonstrated that the three quasi-particle case is manageable using the new approach Soffer and Wu (2023b). It is also possible that the proof of the free channel wave operator exists in the N-body case, leaving the task of proving the absence of weakly localized solutions for initial conditions in the Hilbert subspace of the continuous spectrum of the Hamiltonian. This aspect may necessitate the development of numerous new propagation estimates.

accepted.question_text: For other evolution systems such as Boltzmann-type equations, including singular realistic kernels, or dispersive and fluid-type equations in Fourier space, what hypotheses on asymptotic solutions and what definitions of channel wave operators make scattering-theoretic large-time analysis possible?

evidence.quote: 14.6. Other Classes of Equations. Many other systems may exhibit large-time behavior amenable to scattering theory methods. However, in these cases, one needs a working hypothesis about the form of asymptotic solutions, and an idea of how to introduce appropriate channel wave operators. As demonstrated in the section on self-similar solutions, the corresponding ”asymptotic dynamics” may involve a simple scaling transformation with ”time” represented by α lnt. Interesting cases include Boltzmann-type equations, with or without singular (i.e., realistic) Kernels. Other notable examples involve dispersive equations in the Fourier space of the equation, as encountered in fluid dynamics.

accepted.question_text: For a Schrödinger or wave equation with a known localized smooth potential profile V moving by a Galilean boost, V(x,t) = V(x - vt), how can one determine the unknown velocity v from scattering data? In the free-channel formulation, if measurements determine Ω*u(0) in U(t)u(0) ≃ U0(t)Ω*u(0) for large time and V(x) is known, how can v be recovered?
accepted.context_brief: Inverse scattering for moving potential velocity

evidence.quote: First, consider boost transformations: V =V (x−vt), wherex,v ∈ Rn Beceanu and Soffer (2019). The question here is how to deduce v from the Scattering Matrix. The potentialV is assumed to be a localized and smooth function for simplicity.
Our measurements determine Ω ∗u(0). We also know (say) V (x). How to find v?

accepted.question_text: For a short-lived perturbation W(x,t) added to a stationary potential V0(x), with V(x,t) = V0(x) + W(x,t) and W(x,t) = 0 for |t| > 1, can the scattering matrix determine the time-dependent perturbation W?

evidence.quote: Problem 2 Short-Lived Potential Suppose first that the target is an object centered at the origin, which at time zero start moving to the point (1,1,1) and then come back after a finite time and is at rest forever. This is an example of a short lived potential. So, the general question is, given a potential of the form V (x,t ) = V0(x) +W (x,t ), W = 0 for |t|> 1.
Can the scattering matrix determine W ? See Kian (2017).

accepted.question_text: For a potential whose time dependence is known and is periodic or quasi-periodic, so that Floquet theory converts the problem into a time-independent formulation and scattering can be proved, what is the correct inverse-scattering theory and what data determine the interaction?
accepted.context_brief: Inverse scattering for periodic or quasi-periodic potentials

evidence.quote: Problem 3- Quasi-Periodic Potential If the time dependence is known, but not linear, then if it is periodic or quasi-periodic, we can turn the problem into a time independent one, using Floquet theory. See e.g. Soffer and Weinstein (1998b). We can prove now the scattering for such problems. How Inverse scattering looks like?

accepted.question_text: If a localized time-independent potential W is added to a linearly moving potential, can the additional reflections caused by W be used to solve the inverse-scattering problem with fewer measurements?

evidence.quote: Problem 4- Combined Terms Potential If one adds a localized time independent potential W to the linearly moving potential, can one use the extra reflections from W to solve the problem with less measurements?

accepted.question_text: For the equation i∂tψ = -∆ψ + W(x)ψ + t^-a V(|x|/t^α)ψ, where W and V are smooth localized functions, both potential components support bound states when added to -∆, α < 1/2 gives a stable self-similar regime, and a = 2α is fixed by mass-critical scaling, can the free-to-free channel scattering operator determine W, V, and α? If it can, what reconstruction method should be used despite the expected non-unitarity caused by weakly localized states?

evidence.quote: Thus, the inquiry arises: Can this constrained scattering matrix determine the potential? Consider the equation: i∂ψ ∂t = − ∆ψ +W (x)ψ +t− aV (|x|/t α )ψ, Where W and V (y) are smooth and localized functions of x and y respectively.
The question then arises: Can the channel scattering operator from free waves to free waves, determines W , V , and α ? If so, how?

accepted.question_text: Do existing small-data inverse nonlinear scattering results for nonlinear Schrödinger equations with potentials and polynomial nonlinearities hold in sufficient generality to determine complex nonlinear systems from small scattering experiments, and can large-data free-channel wave operators or free-to-free scattering matrices recover the Born-type information needed to determine the interaction terms?

evidence.quote: Therefore, if it can be shown that the Born approximation is uniquely determined by the Free Channel Wave Operator or by the free-to-free Scattering matrix, the results follow.

The first question of interest is whether the above results hold in sufficient generality. This would be significant, implying that small data scattering experiments can determine the complex structure of nonlinear systems.

accepted.question_text: In nonlinear or multichannel scattering, how can one determine the energies or range of localized asymptotic solutions from the matrix corresponding to free-to-free channel scattering? In particular, in systems such as photon scattering from a multi-particle atom, is observing only a free photon in and a free photon out sufficient to determine all asymptotic channels and localized components?

evidence.quote: Problem 1 How can the energies (range) of localized solutions be determined? Is it possible to ascertain this based on the construction of the matrix corresponding to free-to-free channel scattering?

Even if our observations are restricted to cases with a photon in and a photon out, and even if we limit ourselves to the subspace of the continuous spectrum (of the three-body problem), some states will have three free particles out and some only a bound state and a free photon. Is it feasible to determine everything solely by observing the photon?

accepted.question_text: In a setting with no localized bound-state solutions, such as a non-negative localized smooth potential perturbed by a defocusing nonlinear term where one expects global existence and no localized solutions beyond known small-data cases, can one construct the scattering matrix and use it to recover both the potential and the nonlinear term?

evidence.quote: Problem 2 Let us consider a simpler situation where there are no bound states solutions to the in the equation. For example, it is expected (still open) that if a non-negative localized smooth potential is perturbed by a defocusing nonlinear term, there will be global existence and no localized solutions in many cases. Certainly, this is known for small initial data. So, there should be no problem in constructing the Scattering Matrix and finding the Potential and the nonlinear term as well.

accepted.question_text: For nonlinear systems such as a double-well potential in any dimension with an added nonlinear term, how can the corresponding resonances be determined from inverse scattering data, and how can the value of the nonlinear Fermi Golden Rule be recovered from the S-matrix?
accepted.context_brief: Nonlinear resonances and Fermi Golden Rule from S-matrix

evidence.quote: If we take a double well potential in any dimension and add a nonlinear term, how can we find the corresponding resonances? This problem involves complex dynamics where the structure of the potential governs and produces solitons Barak et al. (2008); Dekel et al. (2007, 2009). In direct scattering, we know how to handle it in some cases, using the notion of the nonlinear Fermi Golden Rule. But for inverse scattering, how can we find the value of the FGR from the S-matrix?

accepted.question_text: Can there be resonances that are purely nonlinear, generated by nonlinear interactions rather than by a linear Hamiltonian, such as long-lived interactions among two or more solitons before they separate or merge? If such lifetimes appear as resonances in scattering, how can they be recovered from the scattering matrix?

evidence.quote: Problem 3 The question above raises the possibility that there are resonances which are purely nonlinear: driven by purely nonlinear interaction terms. How can this happen? Imagine a nonlinearity which has soliton solutions. It can occur that two or more solitons interact for a long time with each other, before separating or merging. The lifetime of such a process will show up as a resonance in the scattering. How can we find it from the Scattering Matrix?

accepted.question_text: Can adding a background potential, mirror, or active medium to a nonlinear scattering system improve the inverse problem and reduce the required data by creating extra reflected information, and can one construct a rigorous example where the S-matrix determines both the target and the added mirror while separating waves due to the nonlinearity from waves due to the background potential?

evidence.quote: Problem 4- Adding a Background Potential to a Given System Adding an extra potential or changing the background from a vacuum to something active may enhance the quality of solving the inverse problem, as well as reduce the amount of data needed Barsi et al. (2009).

The crucial point is that the S matrix also determines the mirror! Therefore, by separating (mathematically or experimentally) the waves coming from the nonlinearity and the mirror W , one gets two observations of the target from different directions, in just one measurement. A rigorous construction of such an example would be great!

accepted.question_text: For a Schrödinger operator H = H0 + V(x) = -∆ + V(x) with localized time-independent potential and complete bounded wave operators Ω±, how can compactness of localized outgoing wave-operator expressions be related to transmission eigenvalues? Can one prove discreteness of the transmission-eigenvalue set, use approximate knowledge of Ω to construct candidate transparent frequencies k, and extend the method to time-dependent or nonlinear interactions?

evidence.quote: The question is how to use these observations to relate it to the notion of transmission eigenvalues ? Can one use the above compactness to prove the discreteness of the set of transmission eigenvalues? Knowing Ω, even approximately, how to get an approximate candidate for transparent k? We know how to construct Ω for time dependent and nonlinear interactions. How to use this knowledge for the construction of transparency?

accepted.question_text: Can one prove exponential spatial decay of localized solutions for a general class of nonlinear equations and time-dependent potentials, beyond known pointwise decay in dimensions five and higher and known smoothness or boundedness of all powers of the dilation operator A in some purely nonlinear dispersive settings?

evidence.quote: Problem 1- Exponential Decay of Localized Solutions Can one prove exponential decay of the localized solutions of a general class of nonlinear equations and time dependent potentials? We have already shown that in 5 or more dimensions the solutions have some pointwise decay in x. We also know, quite generally that Anψ is uniformly bounded in L2 for all n for purely nonlinear equations (e.g. Inter-critical in 3 or more dimensions) and that the solution is smooth.

accepted.question_text: For general scattering problems with a projection Psc onto scattering states, can Psc be characterized in terms of the asymptotic energy operator H+ by the identity Psc = P(H+ ≥ 0) - P(H+ = 0)? What sufficient and necessary conditions ensure P(H+ = 0) = 0, meaning absence of weakly localized states, and can local decay on the range of Psc be proved in dimensions three and four?
accepted.context_brief: Projection onto scattering states and asymptotic energy

evidence.quote: This projection operator is an important object in many ways. Its range is the set of all initial data that are pure scattering states for large time. On its range we expect Local Decay, Strichartz estimates and more to hold.
Is it true that Psc =P (H + ≥ 0) − P (H + = 0)? Find sufficient conditions for P (H + = 0) = 0 , implying the absence of weakly localized states.

Find necessary conditions for P (H + = 0) = 0 . The above limit defines a self-adjoint operator H +. Can one prove that Local Decay holds on the range of Psc also in three and four dimensions? What would be a useful analog in the nonlinear case?

accepted.question_text: Under what sufficient or necessary conditions are the asymptotic states in a general nonlinear scattering problem exact solutions of the equation determined by the asymptotic dynamics? In particular, if an asymptotic state is reached rapidly as t tends to infinity, is that rate of convergence sufficient to imply that the asymptotic state is an exact solution?

evidence.quote: Problem 3- The nature of Asymptotic States In linear multi-channel scattering theory, part of the notion of AC is that the asymptotic parts are moving independently. In particular, they are solutions of the equation defined by the asymptotic dynamics. This is not true for general nonlinear equations. Can one find sufficient conditions implying that the asymptotic states are also exact solutions of the equation? One soliton plus radiation satisfies this condition, but 2 solitons plus radiation may not Martel and Merle (2011), though in this case the asymptotic state is a linear combination of two exact solutions. Find necessary conditions. In particular, suppose the asymptotic state is reached fast as t goes to infinity. Is it sufficient?

accepted.question_text: For inverse acoustic scattering by an object immersed in a fluid, must the fluid flow be known or solved in order to reconstruct or see the object, especially when the object moves with the fluid and its position carries information about the fluid state?
accepted.context_brief: Inverse acoustic scattering in a moving fluid

evidence.quote: Problem 4- Back to Leonardo Da Vinci Do we need to know the flows in the medium to solve the inverse problem? Using E.M. waves, as they can move in a vacuum, this question does not apply. We consider then, an object immersed in a fluid and being observed by acoustic waves. Do we need to know the flow? Clearly, if the object is moving in the fluid, the position of the object says something about the fluid state. Can we ”see” the object without solving for the waves (and vortices, etc.) of the fluid?
